To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the temperature distributions in dense cores are not uniform and that the temperature distribution in the center of a dense core can have a significant effect on the emission from the dust.

the submillimeter continuum data are well fitted by Bonnor-Ebert density distributions with temperatures that decline in the center of the cores, that these density distributions are consistent with contraction, and that the cores appear to be in an evolutionary sequence.
preprotostellar sources have low central dust temperatures and that the dust emission is consistent with a centrally condensed Bonnor-Ebert sphere.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of low-mass star forming regions in the submillimeter and centimeter wavelength range.
the study of the mass of preprotostellar dense cores and the evolution of the density distribution in such cores.
the study of the physical properties of the dense gas and dust in preprotolar and protostellar cores.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are consistent with the cores being singular isothermal spheres with constant density regions of ~0.2 core radius.
the cores are in a state of collapse and are contracting toward the formation of a star.
the preprotostellar core L1544 is a Bonnor-Ebert sphere with a central density ~10^7 cm^-3, a radius ~0.02 pc, and a mass of ~0.1 Msun.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the submillimeter dust emission traces the mass distribution in preprotostar cores.
the submillimeter data for preprotostars can be fit by models of contracting, centrally condensed Bonnor-Ebert sphere cores.
the dust emission is consistent with the hypothesis of low-mass star and brown dwarf formation by contraction and collapse of preprotostellar condensations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dust emission from preprotospherical cores can be modeled with Bonnor-Ebert sphere models.
the dust temperature distribution in preprotosteller cores can have a strong effect on the dust emission.
the dust emission from these cores is not a good indicator of the underlying density distribution.
